demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
It was a Tuesday afternoon in late October when the branch manager asked Dan to help with the coin-counting machine. The customer, a heavyset man in a work vest, had been waiting, and Dan, rushing to clear the line, reached past him to grab the roll of quarters. His elbow caught the customer’s arm, which was resting on the counter’s edge, and in the awkward lurch the man’s hand slipped, his wedding ring catching the lip of the teller window. The skin tore; blood ran down the counter and pooled in the coin tray. Dan stood frozen, staring at the red spread, while the customer swore and the manager called for a first-aid kit. The man needed four stitches. Dan heard that later from the branch secretary. He never saw the customer again. But he could not stop seeing that hand, the way the ring had dragged, the wet sound of the blood hitting the metal tray. The memory came in fragments—the glint of the ring, the sudden darkening of the fabric on the man’s sleeve, the smell of copper—and each piece carried a wave of terror that felt as fresh as the moment itself, followed by a dull, grinding guilt that sat in his chest for hours afterward.

In the weeks that followed, Dan found himself unable to relax. Even at home, in his recliner with the television on, his shoulders stayed tight and his eyes kept moving to the front door. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert; he lay in bed listening for footsteps, for the sound of someone coming to accuse him. He was superalert at work, scanning every customer’s hands as they approached his window, watching for rings, for the way someone might rest an arm on the counter. The vigilance exhausted him, and the exhaustion made the memories sharper. Each time a fragment surfaced—the ring, the blood, the sound—his body reacted as if it were happening again, which only reinforced his sense that he could not let his guard down. He had come to believe that he was inadequate, that he had permanently changed for the worse, that his reactions since the event proved he was a lousy coper. This belief made him more watchful, more certain that he needed to anticipate danger, because if he failed again he would not be able to bear it. The hypervigilance also meant that he noticed every small stressor—a customer raising their voice, a manager calling his name sharply—and each of these moments confirmed his inadequacy, tightening the loop.

Dan had been a teller for thirty-one years. He knew the rhythm of the lobby, the faces of the regulars, the way the light fell across the counters in the afternoon. Now that rhythm was gone. He avoided standing near customers who wore rings, and he flinched when anyone touched him without warning—a colleague clapping his shoulder, a customer handing him cash and brushing his fingers. He had started to believe that the people he knew, his regulars, might somehow know what he had done, that they could see the guilt on him. The stress of each interaction fed his sense of permanent damage, and that sense, in turn, made every future interaction feel loaded with potential failure. He had stopped going to the break room because someone might sit too close. He had stopped talking to his wife about his day because he could not find the words for what he felt. The only thing that seemed to quiet the fragments was staying watchful, but the watchfulness kept the fragments alive.

What finally brought Dan to seek help was a morning in late January when a customer—a woman in a red coat, her hand resting on the counter—asked him a simple question about a deposit, and he could not answer. His mouth opened but no sound came. He stood there, staring at her hand, and the terror rose so fast that he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he sat on the floor for twenty minutes, shaking. His manager sent him home. His wife made the appointment. Dan does not know if he can change what he is now. He is afraid that the damage is permanent, that he is inadequate, that he will never be able to stand at the window again without seeing the blood. But he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not try.
